newsitem.title: UK: Short stg futures see 50 bp rate rise from Labour.
newsitem.headline: Short stg futures see 50 bp rate rise from Labour.

text.p: Britain's ruling Labour government will bite the bullet and produce a half point interest rate rise almost immediately after taking power, according to the interest rate futures strip, analysts said on Friday.

Short sterling interest rate futures are betting Chancellor-in-waiting Gordon Brown will opt for a chunky 50 basis point rise rather than a quarter point hike after his first meeting with Bank of England Governor Eddie George.
And the rate rises will not stop there, as the government tries to keep a lid on the robust British economy and buff up its credentials as a prudent inflation-buster, they said.
"I think the market is moving towards a half point move next week rather than a quarter," Adam Cole, UK economist at HSBC James Capel in London said.

"At the last monetary meeting when the Bank was pushing for a quarter all the key indicators they were looking at -- earnings, broad money, GDP growth -- have moved against the Chancellor's position as it was then," he said. "For that reason, I think the Bank will actually push for a half and I see no reason for Brown not acquiescing."
British base rates currently stand at six percent.

At 0952 GMT, June short sterling futures were quoted down 0.01 at 93.36, discounting interest rates of around 6.64 percent by expiry. Further down the strip, September futures were quoted at 93.13, seeing rates of 6.87 and and December futures at 92.94, factoring in rates of 7.06 percent.
Short sterling futures reflect market expectations of where three month money rates will be at expiry. Three month money has traditionally tracked base rates.

The sheer size of Labour's victory caught British markets by surprise. Labour has clinched 417 seats so far, giving them a clear majority over the Conservatives with 160 seats and the Liberal Democrats at 41.
Short sterling futures dipped early, unnerved by the scale of the Labour victory. Rates of seven percent by the end of the year were reflected in the market.

"There's a feeling Labour could even get away with a full point rise and blame the Tories. That's caused the short sterling strip to discount rates at seven percent by December," said a trader at a British brokerage.
Cole at HSBC did not expect the Chancellor to raise rates more than 50 basis points in one go but saw rates heading higher by year end.
"I would certainly look for more in the course of the year and more out into 1998 as well. For the time being the front month contract is about right," he added.
Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives at Cooperative Bank in London, said the short sterling strip may have got a little ahead of itself.

"The market was already looking for a half...but I think a quarter is more likely and then they can reflect and see if they need to do it again," Beauchamp said. "The market may be getting a little overdone here. If it does drift down a little bit lower I would probably be saying it's advisable to then go into it."

Kirit Shah, chief market strategist at Sanwa International in London, said it was typical for the market to overestimate rate rises. He expected an increase of 50 basis points over the next two to three months.
"For me the risk was that if it was a strong Labour majority they might not raise rates," he said, adding they may favour a weaker pound to protect exporters.
Analysts said U.S. interest rate policy would be the driving factor for the market.

U.S. April payrolls were key on Friday after a week of conflicting economic signals out of the U.S. All markets would be focused on the May 20 monetary policy meeting of the Federal Reserve and the possibility of further interest rate rises.
